blocks.x: I made my first communion at Carver's Christmas. I was living on St. Anne between Miro and Taunty, 23rd, 18th St. Anne. Anybody who knows these men can make them out. Oh, very good picture, very good picture. I'm sure that T.O. could do. I bet you T.O. and I bet you Manette would know a lot of them men. Yeah, very likely.
Boy, I see Manette would know some of them.

Well, you said this man here or this man is not Mr. Sheldon? Let me see. That's not Mr. Sheldon? I can't make a moment. Thank you. Well, if it is, I couldn't recognize him. I know him very well. Well, you should be. But I don't think he's on that. No picture Sheldon. Because I was sitting there just trying to see who could be him. If anybody would be him on it, it would be this man, but that's not him. No. I'm almost sure. This is a good picture of George Moore right here. Yes, indeed.
I think we had a picture. I've never seen a picture of George Moore, I don't believe.
No.
Yes, very good. He was leader of a band quite often. Was it the Excelsior band or something that he had?
I don't know what band. I remember.
I sort of remember. It might be that he was leader of the Excelsior band. Maybe that's what this is. Uh-huh.
Maybe so. You can't read anything on their cap, son.
No. Maybe with a magnifying glass we could, I bet. What was the occasion, do you think, of this? Was it just a, was it started for the parade for the school? They usually have one now, too.
No, I think that was the Sodality meeting. You see the banner? Oh, I see the banner. Yes. It was the Sodality meeting.

Mm-hmm. They have one for the school now, on the Carpus Christi, don't they? And when is that? Early in the spring, usually in April. Mm-hmm. April. It's real early April or May, but near Mother's Day.
Yes, on the roll of the news, cabbage.
I believe it was on Mother's Day last year.
Well, you got these names on tape. You know, it's a beautiful. Montreal, Canada.
Yes. I'm wondering, um, is this a regular brass band, too? Did you see anything on this? My eyes aren't good enough to see. Reading what's on the drum.
No, I can't see it very clearly.
Probably with a magnifying glass.
I can just see the first part of it, that's all.
And I wondered if there was any...

There's something on there. Oh. Let me see. I can see the top part, but I can't see the bottom part. Um, Martin's Big Revival. I can see. Martin's? Yes, M-A-R-T-O-N apostrophe S. Of J.C. Stewart's. Stewart's. Mm-hmm. J.C. Stewart's. You can see that, huh? Mm-hmm. And it says here, nothing but... what? Well, that's what I couldn't see. That's what it is. Nothing but fun, I guess. F-U-N, fun. Yes, that's what it looks like. Nothing but fun. Mm-hmm. You have something comedy. Yes, right in here. Yeah, you can see. Like you say, maybe with a microscope you could make it out. Yeah. Mm-hmm. They look like firemen there, don't they? Yeah, they look like helmets. That's the one I told... I wonder who this fella is. He's... Might be the manager or something. Mm-hmm. Oh, I kept telling you you had a picture with him in a fireman's uniform. I could remember those helmets. Mm-hmm. They look just like firemen. I suppose actually it's some kind of a comedy show, I suppose, they're playing for. And his leggings, they use leggings, you see? Yeah, leggings. Mm-hmm. November 26th, 1970. Yeah, I was born. I was just a few months old when he had that picture name. Yeah, Monday night. I was born in March.
This one with all the trees, it looks like it could be either in a park or in the country. It could be, yeah. Was this around New Orleans, do you think?
No, no, there's none of these pictures taken in New Orleans.
Except this one big one here.
This one, yes.
So it might be near Milwaukee, you think, or someplace?
I don't know where that one was taken. It was sent to me.
You don't remember where that came from?
It must be Milwaukee. Because it doesn't look like anything around here.

Or if it was sent to you, you might have been out on the road with one of these shows, you think? It was sent to me, yeah. Might be that. So the chances are that most of these fellows might not be from New Orleans then, I guess. Yes. Oh, I hardly think.
With the trees, it may not have been. I don't think these fellows are from New Orleans either. Or the ones from Canada.
No, they say it's Canada. Probably a Canadian band.
Mm-hmm.
Does that look like a regular brass band? Papa band. Papa player and all kinds of bands. It's not a dance band. It's not a dance band. They have their uniforms there.
This is a good picture of him too. Yeah. You know, a person that knew him when he was getting older. Yes.
To me it looks different than the others, but I've never seen one of them that old then. That looks different.
That's the last picture.
And he certainly doesn't look old there, but I mean the others are all when he was just a young boy almost.
He was 52. He was 52 when he died.
Did he live to be 52? Yes.
You know, after my father was laid out, he came back almost as young as this.
That 19 year old looked like that.

He really, it was remarkable how he came back to himself. I never think that he was that. He thought he was a young boy in the caucus. Strange. That's why I keep saying this is such a good picture of him because I can picture him, you know, in that casket and how his features came back so perfectly. Yes. Just like he is there. I have to laugh at him because he did everything. He played in all kinds of people. Now here he is in a soldier's uniform. He got in anything. He used to wear some beautiful white and gold uniforms when he played the carnival parades. And my mother used to do stuff He played in all kinds of... Now here he is in a soldier's uniform. He got in anything. He used to wear some beautiful white and gold uniforms when he played the carnival parades. And my mother used to do those things up by hand. Beautiful. They wore white uniforms when they worked for Anderson. I used to do them up. Well they wore tuxedos too. We had the picture. They had to make changes in winter and summer. This is in the tuxedos. They wear the white suit in the summer. In the summer. And the tuxedo in the winter.
Would that be the one in the band with Paula Barber and Albert Nicholas? I showed you, yes.
We have Albert Nicholas.
Yes, we had a copy of that picture already. They used to play together too in Chicago. In Chicago too.

He gave Albert lessons. Remember on St. Philip's Dream? Why I remember so very well that he gave him lessons is because I was quite young. And he was a young sailor and he was very good looking. And I ran inside and put ribbon in my hair. And Karen sat in the front row and my daddy ran me out. That's what makes me remember him so very well. He was a fine looking sailor coming in. That was the first world war.
Yeah. I remember. I knew him in New York around 1940 to 1945, along that period. He was a good looking man too. He was a fine looking man.
He was a fine looking man. The last I heard him in Chicago. Yes, that's the last I heard him in Chicago.

He came to this country about two years ago, a little over a year ago. And I don't think he ever got to New Orleans. He went to California and he was in Chicago. He's been living in France and Belgium for quite a while. Oh, for five to ten years almost. More? Oh, wow. He just made a quick clip over here about a year ago, a little over a year ago I think.

Oh, they were supposed to go to China. I was in China. You were in the town, Papa? That's what I was saying. He went to China. He went to China. But my father was supposed to go too, he got sick. He was planning, it was planning that he would go along too to China. They were in Chicago at that time. Yes. They were supposed to go to China. But he didn't go, he came back here. Most naturally he was sick, he came home. Yes. But that was one of his ambitions though, to get to China. That we see the whole world. He had, we had all kinds of rocks and different souvenirs that he brought from different places that he traveled. Wood, you know. Petrified, for us would. We had all kinds of rocks and different things from different places that he visited. Yes. He would bring something back. And just from the years that got rid of him. I was wondering if you still had his mouthpiece or whatever. Oh no. I had him around here for a long time, got tired of him throwing at the junk. I had no use for him. It's just like his book. He used to write out his own parts, conic parts. And we kept it a while for the title of the old song, you know. And got tired of him throwing out.
Too bad because those are of historic importance now, of course.
That's what I said, if you only knew that. You never know with the title. Many pictures too, different pictures we did away with.
Some musicians keep scrapbooks too, but hardly any of them save them very long. No. After their death they're usually thrown out or lost or somebody.

We kept them for quite a while, but after a few years past. My mother's got disgusted. Having that laying around there. And having a use for it. And we had to rid of them. At the corner of the mouthpiece was a steady machine drawing, then throwing somewhere else and I said, well throw it out. He had no use for it.
Did he put those notches on all of his mouthpieces? I mean even in his late years?
He only had two mouthpieces.
He saved it all the time.
Keep that in his pocket. Never put it down. Never leave it on his home. He treasured that thing.
Yes. But even the last mouthpiece he had, did he have those notches filed in?
Yes, yes he had.
It was three notches.

Three notches he had on them. And then he used to take that hair file and go down there and just open that. Keep it clean. No, no it was to enlarge it. Enlarge it, make a bigger bore. At the bottom, but not on the top because he had, it was very small. He never did use just an ordinary mouthpiece. He said it was too wide and too heavy, you know, for him. And he'd always have it made. And after he had it made, well he'd fix it the way he wanted. He'd file and put the reedges on it. Yeah. And any time he'd sit down, he'd be working on that mouthpiece, you know, and look like, I don't know. He just treasured that thing. Yeah, yeah.
He must have loved his music as you say. He did. He really loved music.

And he'd never leave his horn nowhere else. Anywhere he was, his horn had to be with him. Sometimes people say, why don't you leave your horn if you're not going home now? Uh-uh. Take it with me. I can carry it. Stick it under his arm. Cover it on. Never, never, uh, lend nobody his mouthpiece. Never. But he, when, if he'd borrow a horn, he'd... He'd never use the, the mouthpiece, the horn. No. Take that one off and put his on. Put his. Well he could borrow a horn, John. He played, uh, you know something about him, Harry. Uh-huh. He played from his lips, was that what you called it? Yes. Playing from the lips? Until he had a kernel right there.
Some trumpet players do that. They get a little hard callus. Well he never had that. He had a, he'd get a blister.
It was hard right there. But he never.
The whole lip gets a little bit hard. I mean the muscle develops. No, but it was right here. On the lower lip.
On his lower lip, yeah. And he used to put, uh, antiseptic. He always kept that poison with antiseptic. It's all he used to know.
Remember a friend of mine, Buck Johnson, always used Dr. Tishner's antiseptic. That's that, that's why he's Tishner's. Always rubbing on his lips.

Yeah. Always rubbing on his lips. Mm-hmm. Yeah. Carried that with him. Mm-hmm. And when he was at home he'd have a little piece of cotton, you know, and just put it on his lips like that little bit of a thing. I'll tell him Mr. Russell, he never had swelling in the face.
He'd puff out his cheeks.

Oh, he had a little boy that he was teaching him, a little boy on, uh. Roman Street. On Roman Street. Oh, he used to take interest in that little child. I could hear him telling that, uh, that, that little boy, don't blow bubbles. He said, blow from here, from your chest. From your chest. And then he'd be saying, hold your mouthpiece, take your, take your mouthpiece off your corner. Make him take it off and he'd hold it like that. Oh, yeah. Just try it alone, without the... Amity shell. Mama, tell him, you said he used to give lessons just on the... Oh, this, uh, Tony Salazar, you know him, huh? Yeah. He used to take amity shell lessons from him. Just blow on the horn. From the mouthpiece. Just to teach him the whole, his mouthpiece on his lips, you know. Used to come again. I don't know what that was called, 19-something. He got a barbershop on his chest. He took lessons from him in a long time. Oh, he gave him quite a few people around here. About 25, 27, I believe. Yeah. I'm looking at this, does the show look like a little match on it? It does, huh? Oh, oh. Really good.
Maybe we can find somebody else that could identify it. Yeah.

I'm sure, Mr. Downey Clancy. If I can walk out there tomorrow, I'm going to ask him. Who? Mr. Till. Mr. Till. To you. And give the names. Give the names. You know I'm going to put them on a knee down and make a little arrow, you know, right to them. Yeah.
Uh-huh. Or some people write it on the back of the picture. Yes, they do. If it's light enough shade, it can be written on it. Right there. Back, just who they are, then people wouldn't forget.
Uh-huh. That's a good way to do it, huh?
Well, we don't want to bother you any longer. There's no problem. Unless there's something else that you can think of about Mr. Ntoyun that you'd like to tell before we...
Well, that's about all right now. I think that covers... More than all, different places he went to play that I really can't remember. Oh, if you never remember every place he played.
And stuff like
Because as I tell you, he'd tell me I'm going there tonight. Well, you're just going. You'll be back. It's all right, you know. And I never paid attention to it.
I would have paid just about every place that was, I suppose.
Yeah.
And we certainly enjoyed seeing the pictures and talking through here and hearing. Very nice pictures.
Thank you very much.
I'm just sorry I don't have more. I could have more.
I'm trying to find where they're trying to play. I will. I'm interested in them too much. Yeah.
Yeah, the clarity has a fact that figure is. Let's take the jump right out. I'll have it run on through here. I have to accept this box.
You know what you can do, Helen? You can send one of the boys. And it's going to give you the name of the musician that he knows on there. Then we can give it to you, huh?
Yeah. Yeah, and I'll pass him. Pick it up on you so he can know who it is.
Yeah. We'll try to find out and get the names to you.
We're going to go back to see you one day next week. One evening next week we're going over there.
We'll get it.
Yeah.
And we can talk to him about it then. Yeah. Yeah.
But if you have the picture while they'll be there, I'll run over you and get it.
Pick up the names and we can get them. Well, I'll tell you what we could do, Mama. You could leave Glenn take it over there too, Mr. T.

And let it stand there until you all get there. Yeah, until we get there. That's right. And then he can go back and get it. Because there might be somebody he has to think about on that. I saw a member of Shani's family and they're asking to give Shani's right name for me.
These are the pictures. Let's see. That's a good picture.
This is the one. That's the old-time coronet. This is your husband.
Yes.
Isn't that a good picture?
Oh, yeah. He's holding his little shark coronet. Look at that. See? He was quite young there. He looks like about 20 years old actually, doesn't he?
And this is the one. I told you about him in unicorns. That's right. He's in the sun. He's playing trouble too. Oh, yes.
This is an owl here. This is sitting there. Right where?

Right here. I can't see him at the night right now. Who can see him? Can you find Sidney out there? That's Rose right there. Oh, yes. Right by the... I think that's right there. I see him here. That's Rose. I know Rose.
He's standing second to the... Last. Oh, last on the end on the right. See the earphones they have? Oh, yes. It's not sure.
It looks like a parman's uniform.

That says Montreal, Canada, Premier Theatre, November 26, 19 and 7. And tonight the two Johns. I guess that's a show or something else. Yes. Some other act. Can you read any more of that, Ralph, on there? Yeah. We'll read what it says on the drum.
It says the Nation's Big Revival of J.C. Stewart's. Let me see. There's a sign on the back that says positively. Oh, no smoking in this room. I couldn't read it very good.
This one says Mitchell Grove, Sunday, August the 4th, 1907. There he is again, right here, in a different uniform.

Oh, yes. That's the small brass band. That's the old generation. And he's down here on the kneeling almost, or sitting on the ground, I guess. Sitting on the ground. This is it. With a big bass drum with a rope. And the snare drum. And right behind Mr. Matoya is a tuba. One, two, three, four, five, six, seven. Only an eight-piece band. I guess two carnets and tuba and trombone. Two drums, alto horn. Oh, that's a baritone there. There. There's the tuba. That's all they had.
And how many do they have in this one?
This is a regular brass band. Eight. Four, five, six. Only eight pieces. I've heard of the old.
They have the baritone.
And the alto horn.
And the upright bass.
Yeah, there's the bass.
Upright bass and baritone. And the alto horn. This is the alto horn. They call it French horn.
No clarinets, I believe.
I don't see them. Two carnets.
Two drummers, of course. Two carnets.
And this is the one the National Soldiers Field in Chicago. That's a late one.
Oh, yes.
Where is it? I want to. No, not that. That's Chicago.
Which is Mr. Matoye. I don't see.
No, right. Right here. He's holding his arm. See him right there? Right there?
Yes.
No, right here.
Oh, yes. On the first, next to the drummer. You recognize him? Sure, I see now.
Yeah, that's right.
Next to the snare drummer.

On the front row. And you remember when I told you about Mama, him going off and going to Tennessee? Oh, yes. This is the last picture of him. It's the last picture. Just before I left. That's the one in Tennessee. They say he was bandmaster.
With the flag there and all. Mm-hmm. Must have been on a big stage, I guess, over here.
Yeah, it was a big stage.
And his picture is up in the little round picture up in the corner of that.
Now, here they are, four generations. That's the one. Remember you were asking me about my grandfather?
Oh, yes.
Well, this is my grandfather, right? That's his father right here.
And he played, too, you see? He played music?

No, he played cornet. His mother, this old lady, played guitar. Oh, I knew it was the guitar. He told her he had some corrections to me. This is his grandmother. My father's, in other words, this is his mother. And this is his son. And this is my brother, which is his son. That's my oldest brother.
That's your oldest brother, little baby.
Four generations.
Baby, oh, yeah.
That's all. Eleven months old. Chani? Yeah. That's Chani. That's Chani. That baby, yeah. Yeah. I was dead in Chicago.
He don't change much.
And here's another picture of my grandfather. He's always been out. He doesn't care.
And he played cornet then, too. Did he play in any of the brass bands here?
I couldn't tell you. Not here. I don't believe it. He spent a lot of his time in Newark.
In Newark.
In Newark. In Newark. In Newark. In Newark. Mexico. He was born in Newark. In Newark. In Newark. Yes, he was a native.
Do you notice the chapel up in Newark?
The one with the little donkey there.
I don't think you saw this one. This is Carpus Christi.
He's right here, too. Carpus Christi Holy Name Society.
Something about New Orleans under there. January. January 1917.
New Orleans, Louisiana.
They took that over here, was it?
Yeah, that's right here. That was in 1917.

There he is. Oh, you mean from the church, right? Yes. That's why I made my first communion. Sure. When he said Carpus Christi, I thought Carpus Christi, Texas, you know. Since he traveled so much, I thought it was in the church.
Yeah, sure. It's the church. There he is. Where is he? Finding that? He's right behind his band. There he is.
That's Anor Land. This is Sidney Desween right here.
Oh, Sidney Desween is almost in the back of the bass drum.
Yeah, Anor is right behind his drum arm. Oh, I'm right behind you.
And he's George Moritz. It was a drum arm.
The trombone looks familiar, too, but I can't think of it. You never hear him, George Moritz? He was a very good trumpet. Yes, I've heard people mention him.
I don't know everybody on there, but...
Yeah?
Is Mr. Shalini on there? Can you find him?
No, I'm trying to see.
Let me count how many are in the band. One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten, eleven, twelve.
He's a seven, eight, nine, nine, nine.
And I see two trombones and the two drums and an alto horn and probably a baritone horn. The two trumpets, three trumpets.
That bass horn? Yeah, upright bass.

Yeah, there's a tuba. That's funny. Don't see a clarinet again. There's somebody playing something there. And those two fellas, I can't see what they're playing. One probably is a clarinet. That's a clarinet there. Could that be T.O. by any chance?
Let me see this.
I'll tell you. Did you all get an interview with T.O.?
Not yet. We haven't called him yet. It'll be well within a day. No, that's not T.O. It's not T.O.
I bet you T.O. can tell him most of him musicianette's on there. Yeah, but that's not T.O.
Yeah, that's not T.O. I bet he's good. I'm a runner. Some people would know a few of the others.
Well, maybe he may be a, how do they call him, a northern man on there.
So we know who the three coronets are, Sidney Desvin, you say? I wonder who this guy is.
Sidney Desvin is a coronet. Yeah.
Morat, a nomorized Sidney Desvin. Sidney Desvin.
I don't know none of those. I think that's proper.
I don't know. The drummer almost looks familiar to me, but I can't think.
This drummer, see this drummer here? He looks very familiar.
I really don't know many of those people on there.
Actually, he looks maybe something like Louis Dumaine to me, though.
I think at the time, Vic Gaspar was playing his drummer for him.
Vic would be one of the two trombones. This is a wonderful trombone.

Oh, but if you know, stare behind that little coronet. Yeah. Someone gave him that little horn, and he had holes in him, you know, and he stopped him up with gum, and the water valve was broke. And he took a piece of carc, and he cut it to fit. And it didn't stay down. He took a rubber band, and he wrapped around there. And they had something else, again, he had to put on it. I just remember now. But nevertheless, he would, whenever he had to clean it, he'd get those BB shots, you know what they call them? Oh, yeah. The little lead pellets. And he'd fill that up, and then he'd have soap water, and just shake that in there until he cleaned it out, and take every valve out. He'd almost stay there half a day, and then he'd have his pencil there, and walk in the valve, and he'd take them out and put the string back, you know?
Oh, yeah. So when you got them mixed up.

Then when he'd take that out, it was so green in there that he had a little brush, and he'd clean that out with the brush. Then when he'd get through with that, then he'd get some perpetua. The horn was so dirty looking, you know, so brassy. He'd make a paste with that, and he'd put it on the horn, and he'd let it dry. Then he'd start to polish, get a rag, and polish, and polish, until he'd get it just the way he wanted. What was that preparation again? Perpato.
Some people use that to clean their teeth with, don't they? My mother used it.

Years ago, that's all he used to do. And how would you put it on that face? Perpato. And then the funny part of it, all stopped up like that, he would play it. He'd go on the job with that. Now you see here, I told you all that he played Night and Day at the Globes Hall, but my mother said it was the Palms. Yeah, he played the Palms. It was the Palms.
Night and Day came out later, I believe, anyway.
And he was 17 years old.
Night and Day would have come out later than that, I believe. But the Palms, that old French piece.

And this old lady there, she was so worried, when he left, he says, I'm going to say a class for you, because you don't know the grace note that you have in that piece, and you're going to make a fool of yourself. She said, why do you want to do that? Why don't you tell them you're sick? She said, I'm gone. And he said it all the way through. He never made one mistake.
Is that the one by the composer? I remember a piece called The Palms by Fauré.
F-A-U-R.
Do you think that's the one?
The Palms. That they use on Easter Sunday.
Yes, that's the one.

That's the one. And it was accompanied by Jenny Jasmine and sponsored by Walter De Silva. Walter De Silva. He used to sponsor quite a bit of concerts in those days. And the concert, the one concert with Ann that have a dance. And then he would play the dance with everybody, broken horn. That's the thing that tickled me. And then he had a file, a round file. And he used to get his mouthpiece made, room walls. But it wasn't shaped. The cup wasn't shaped like the others, you know. It was deep because his mouth was very small. And the mouthpiece had to be very small, so he had made the order. And then he'd file that hole. And then he'd go right in there and keep for hours at the time. And then he'd have the horn there. He'd try to put the mouthpiece on. It wasn't satisfied. He'd go back again, file it again. Then he'd put some ridges on the top of the mouthpiece. Oh, ridges. Yeah, you know, just three ridges on the mouthpiece. I did ask him why did he do that. He said, oh, when I have a triple tongue, that's a big help.
But I keep from slipping when he tripled down. Yeah. And four, so Christ keep it. Yeah. Right across the...
They have three, you see, they're round like this. He put one like this and one like that. And then you file that, you know.
Equally spaced. Yeah. File. No, that's strange to me.

Isn't it strange? Mm-hmm. And he never put his mouthpiece down. It was always in his pocket. Yeah. Whether he played or not, he kept it in his pocket. Well, he believed in that mouthpiece. I was telling you how he used to practice.
To practice. I know other common players ever do that.

Every evening before he'd leave, he'd run his scales. Mm-hmm. And run water in his home. Yeah, always run water in his home. And he'd throw it out before he leaves. Mm-hmm. One time he was very, very sick. You remember when he played for the... For almost this day of the year. Mm-hmm. The first time he went out. Mm-hmm. As weak as he could be. A man came and told him that he had a job. That he said they had a parade. But he didn't have no qual된 stuff. Mm-hmm.

He said, and I came to see how he was feeling. He said, well, how's it around? Long? He said, long? He said, no, not around, just around Canal Street. And we stopped at the Elks place. She said, I'll come. And he went. And his last job, he played on St. Peter and Claiborne. And the man said he played that night like he played as if he was down at the age of 20 years. He said, you don't know what happened to him. He played so well that night. Everybody was noticing, you know, how he was playing that night.
Was that for a dance or a concert or something?
No, it was in a ballroom. I don't know for what reason that was, but I do know they had a ballroom at that place. And, well, that was the last place he played. It was about two weeks before he died.
A week before he died. That's the week before he died.

A week before he died. And during the flu, he was very, very sick. So the doctor told him, he said, now that they were, he was framed with the doctor, you know, and the doctor said, listen, let me tell you something, I know. He said, you're a very, very sick man. And I'm going to pat you up. And I want you to stop smoking, stop drinking, and stop that home. He said, well, doc, I'll stop the smoking, I'll stop the drinking, but I'm going to play until I drop dead. Yeah, he did too. Yeah. Play until he couldn't go anymore. One week after he played, he died. Yeah. Yeah. He loved music then.

Something like Willie. They said that day before, he played that film the day before he died, you know. They say he played that film so beautiful, Willie Pazzo. Oh, Willie Pazzo. They say he played them hymns and played that film like if nothing wasn't wrong with him at all. And the next morning. Yeah, the very night, really during the night. That's right.

And when he used to come and serenade us at 2 o'clock in the morning, where we live now, visit the sacred heart conference. Well, the nuns used to tell the children, the boys, you know, and they were living right in the back of them, who was playing the music last night? He said, we certainly did enjoy that music. It was fine. It was fine. Nobody in the neighborhood complained about him playing. They used to play so low with those music. Yes. You know, it was pretty. It was really pretty. With the old, I mean, when we had that old horn, they wasn't using mute like they're doing now, you know.
He's playing the open horn.
No, not open, the open horn, yes. And he used to, he had an old derby, and he gelt that derby. I said, but you didn't gelt that derby for. And he put it over the bell. Yeah, he put it over there.
Do you remember what kind of pieces they would play out on the, those serenades when they would serenade people?

I can't remember the name of the piece. I think you told me three o'clock in the morning for one. You played three o'clock in the morning, but there was a special waltz they used to play when they go out. But I can't call them. Was it the klema waltz? No, the klema waltz. I can't remember the name.
It was sort of soft, quiet music, like waltz. Very, very soft. Yeah, soft waltz.
And for the old corn egg, he had a tomato can, and he gelt that.
Oh, and use it for a mute.
And just hold it in for, you know, for mute.
Oh, yeah. Oh, and for the bell of the horn.
Yeah, bell of the horn.
I've seen people use water glass or even a coconut shell. Anything to muffle a tone.
And then when you get that wah-wah. Oh, he could do that. You know how to mute, you know, the wah-wah.
He just put his hand over it. Yeah, just use the hand, and somebody should use a toilet flush. Yeah, so it's rubber plungers sometimes. Yeah, plungers.
It used to sound like it was crying, you know, kind of like a baby crying.
He doesn't know how to sound like that. Yes, he could really do that.

I think my brother put all this down. But I told you, you know, one place he played, I didn't tell you about, the Absinthe House. And that Jitney place you were talking about, I think that was... The Lovita? No, I think... He played at the Lovita. I know that. The Music Gods.
I know he played at the Lovita, because he used my trumpet when he played at the Lovita.
Well, he could use it. The Music Gods.
The Music Gods. Yeah, he played there, too. And the foreign name's home. He played at the Alamore. With the foreign, he used to play at the foreign, right?

And he played at Antoine's Restaurant? That's another place. In La Lusanne? La Lusanne, yeah. But you know what he did one time? In fact, that's what he used to do every year. They used to have the Rival King. That was on Monday. On Monday, about 1 o'clock. And they had a parade. So he'd play that parade that day.
Is that when the wrecks would come in on the river?

On the river. They'd go in with the king on the river. And they'd have that parade in the day. Then they'd have the parade at night. And he'd play that night parade. He'd leave the night. When the night parade was over, he'd go to Antoine's Restaurant. He'd play there. Then the next day, he'd play the day parade, which was carnival then. And he'd come home. Then he'd go back for the night parade. And when he'd leave the night parade, he'd go back to La Lusanne. Oh, yeah. And then it was Wednesday morning. He'd get in the bed. Then he couldn't get up the next day at all. No wonder. He was blown up. But you know, he was really a lover of music. He'd play all night on the job, coming around 2, 3 o'clock in the morning. And he had a little crystal set, radio set, with the feeler, you know. And he'd sit in a rocker and sit with that little set until sometimes 7 o'clock in the morning. After playing all night.
Listening to the music.

Just trying to find what he could on that little crystal. He never got tired of music. I don't understand. And then you could hear him to himself, that's a bottle man band. A what? Bottle man. You know the bottle man? Oh, yes. He couldn't stand blasting music. He told you that. He couldn't stand that. He'd come in and say, what's the matter now? He looks so aggravated. He said, oh, we had a rehearsal then. I can't make them fellas understand that they can blow loud and soft. And they're just aggravating. And he said, there's nothing to it. I said, well, there's nothing to it because you know. That's not, if they can't do it. It's true. So you could go up with a high, high note and it would never pierce your ears. Yet it was high. It was soft. Soft. We had to blow. So. We really had that gift of going like that. Oh, yes. Well, sometimes he'd be laying in the bed and she'd be practicing. And he'd tell, uh-uh. We thought he was sleeping. On the piano? Yeah. He said, uh-uh, that's not right. Go over it again. Then he'd get up. He couldn't stand it. He'd start playing the carnet with her. We played him many pieces together.
You were talking Sunday about the band he played in. Was it something like Squires? The carnival band.
It was Jake Steves.
Oh, Steves.
Jake Steves. The Maccabees. The Maccabees.

Steve.
That was his last name. Steve.
Jake Steves. That was his last name. Well, he's dead.
Jake was his first. Jake Steves. Jake and then Steve.
S-T-E-V-E.
Yes.
Steve. And the name of the band was the Maccabees band. Maccabees. I don't know of any of his people. That was a white band. Yes. Yes.
I hadn't heard of it, so I just wondered. You don't know any more about him? If he's still living as a man, Steve, or anybody?
Jake is dead, but he must have some people living. He had a lot of children. And you know who's another good musician, too? Silence. Climate Fair, Piku. All the Pikus.
Yes. We were just talking about him.

They used to play together. In those parades. Yeah, those parades. Well, I think that's how Papa played all the carnival parades, was through Jake Steve. No, I mean Piku used to play. Oh, yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah, it was Jake Steve, the one who had the contract. And he would be, you know, the leading. Oh, he always played the first horn. The first. Carnet, whatever. In those days they called it the carnet.
I wonder, did he ever talk about who his teacher was, or if he had more than one teacher? Well, no.
He, uh...
Or he went to school, or anything to learn with Carnet?
Well, no. He took it up with a relation of him by the name of Oscar Giovanni. Oscar Giovanni. Mm-hmm. But he never had no regular teacher. He just picked it up himself.
Most of them picked it up himself.

Because, uh, his grandmother, this old lady, said that he, uh, even when he was playing as a child, he'd get clothespins and make a carnet, you know? Oh, I like that. And he'd play on top the other day, and he'd just play that, put two on the top and try to... That guy is a carnet. ...bella carnet, you know, and he'd play from a child. And you did tell me that he took a few lessons with, uh... Shalini. Shalini. You know, off and on, people that knew more than him, you know, he would go around then. But I don't know of him having any teaching. And then he would go with, uh, with old men, could be his father at the time. And, you know, and play, stand around and play with them. And, well then at that time he was playing without no music, you see? Yes. He was playing by ear. It's when he left here, that's where he began to play, you know, and read it. Right, music very well. And study harmony and everything. And he'd sit down there with a book all night. He had to have a teacher because he knew music too well.
Oh yes, he must have studied music.

Because he could take a 16, a 64, a 32, And he had a second note from the eights. He knew all of that. Yeah. And he studied all that, you see. But he, Mama says it was after he went away. He played very well, even before he studied that, he must have played very well. Yeah.
And we know that the Levita had stack of music. Well he could read music. Oh yeah. Everybody knows that. Oh yeah. Yes.

He used to have that on the space shelf. Well I knew the music. Because you see, he could read music, you know. But he would take, to hold his music on that little horn there, a clothespin. I said, what, you gonna wash tonight? He said, no. He said, no, I wanna hold up the fans going my music on. Oh yeah, yeah.
Yeah, some people use those on the music rack, they clip it. Quite a few people do that.

You see, evidently, when he, after he'd learned to read music was when he began playing with these bands. But there was a big band, all the way through the band. The band, well he didn't have a band. You don't have anything of him when he was with Barnum and Bailey, huh? No, no. Well he was with them five years. He traveled with them all that time. Five years, yeah. He traveled all that time. And that's what I wanted to tell you. My mother told me he used to play for the races. Oh yeah, he played in the band, but he was the one that would blow the bugle. Oh, the bugle.
I like to have it at the fairground. I still have it at the fairground. He'd be the one that blew the bugle. Yes.

I remember that. I forgot to tell you that. Oh yeah. And he used to blow tap for the veteran, huh? He was in the band too, but he was the one that blew tap. In Milwaukee. In Milwaukee. In Milwaukee. He was in two veterans fans.

Yeah. That's what they used to call it. But they gave him the $25 just for playing that. Yes.
On that mouthpiece. And he also used to get tips for himself when he'd get through playing and the actors would come in at Anderson and he'd play for them to sing and they'd tip him to play.

It was two brothers. It was two brothers.

I was wondering if you would mind Mrs. Matoye telling us something a little bit about yourself. If you don't mind even telling your age, I mean.
Oh, my age. I was 77 on the 26th day of February.
And what was your maiden name?
Fernandez, Virginia Fernandez.
There's one musician I know from that family. Was it a musical family that you came from too? Well, no. Anyone in your family? No. Your father or brothers or anyone?
No. They liked music, but none of them was musical. Yes.
Had you heard much music when you were young before you met Mr. Matoye?
Well, yes, we used to go to the French opera, you know. It's about all the place they had at the time, you know. I like music very much, but I don't know anything about it.
I just wondered if you might have learned some instruments yourself. You never did. Did you sing? Yes. You told me I think Sunday that you could sing.

Very nice voice. Well, I used to sing for myself, you know. I enjoyed it. Sure. But we are a musical family. I don't have to play it, but we do love music. Yes. There's any kind, like I told you before, there's any kind of music that you can find. It's in our collection. We have all the songs. And all the boys sings. Yeah.
That's wonderful that you all have that interest in you.

She has a boy to sing, Ave Maria, what age? Twelve, huh? Merlin? Merlin. Oh, he used to sing, when he was single, he sang a lot of weddings and church affairs. He used to do a lot of that. And he sang in some place in San Francisco, and they wanted to hire him immediately, but his wife didn't want it. He couldn't. And who was the man who wanted to take him away when he was 16? When he was 16. They wanted to take him to see this fellow who interviews. He had a show this summer called The Talent Show. Not Arthur Godfrey, the other one. No, I don't have a talent show. The little fat one. You know the shot Fat One? Just this summer he had a talent show. They wanted to put him in. I wouldn't let him go, because he was only 16. I didn't know anybody in New York. I didn't want him to go. But we all love music. Just, you know, I don't know. Just musical family. Even the little babies that my little grandchildren, you should hear him sing with the radio. He just sings, picks up every word, just one right after him. Just one right after him. Carry the melody, and he's only three years old. So maybe we'll get a musician out of him.
Maybe another musician, famous musician, come out of the family sometimes.

Well, my husband intended to make a musician out of her oldest son, but he didn't live long ago. He said, I'm going to make a musician out of him. I'll connect the out of him. I tried it. I had him for a year, but he suffered with high blood pressure when he was just 12 years old, and the doctor told me it wouldn't be very good for him. So I just dropped the blowing. And that's what he wanted. Now, I have my younger son who loves the piano. And I've never, it's just, I don't know why. I guess by me not being well, I never did see that he had lessons. But until today, he still wishes to play the piano. It looks like it's in him, you know. He would like it very much. So, there's just about all the information we have on him.
